title: Breaking the Box
author: John Danner
summary: John Danner compares his early years building the Rocketship charter network with his current work at Flourish, a network of AI-enabled private schools funded through state reimbursement. The box he wants to break is whatever caps a network's program quality or its ability to scale. On quality, he argues that owning the product, rather than renting vendor edtech as a black box, lets Flourish ship a dozen improvements a day and tie product and program into a single loop. AI also lets the Writing app replace point-and-click exercises with real student writing and real feedback. On scale, he lists the political frictions that held Rocketship to about 25 percent annual growth: chartering hearings, regulatory oversight and real estate fights. His claim is that state-reimbursed private networks avoid both constraints, and that a specified, measured program lets quality hold as the network grows.
points: Owning the product rather than being one buyer among hundreds lets a school network change software daily in response to what happens in classrooms.
AI makes it feasible to grade real student writing at scale, which shifts the Flourish Writing app from clicking exercises toward about 20 minutes of writing a day with feedback.
Charter growth was throttled by politics (hearings, oversight, real estate obstruction), whereas state-reimbursed private networks mainly face registration and accreditation.
Small sites cost about $250k and open in months, compared with roughly $10m and two years for a typical Rocketship building.
Tight integration of product and program lets the network specify and measure the work of its least experienced staff, so quality can improve rather than dilute with growth.
quotes: Rocketship Learning Lab was great, an operationalizing of 1-1 learning through edtech products. But we didn’t own the products, couldn’t manipulate them, they were basically black boxes.
But then we realized that students improve by writing, not clicking. Everybody in education knows that. Almost nobody built it, because grading real student writing at scale wasn’t possible.

It was an engine built for 100% annual growth forever. Politics created massive friction that slowed that 100% down to a max of about 25% annual growth, which we achieved when we played the politics perfectly.
A school that can’t open in August doesn’t open until the next August. Every delay was worth a full year to them, and it only had to work some of the time.
Average Rocketship buildings cost $10m and took two years. Average Flourish sites cost $250k and take a few months.
What’s changed is the tight integration of product and program. The program is specified and measured now, and the product drives and measures the school day in a way we never had at Rocketship.

Private school networks with state reimbursement don’t have either constraint. That’s a different thing, and I think it’s the best mechanism anybody has built for giving all children a good school option.
